note: Machine-readable IOC set consumed by tools/. Defensive detection only. Never resolve, fetch, or connect to any indicator listed here.

families.name: Blum Panel (FiveM extortion / server-lock backdoor)
behaviour: Injects a hidden server_script into fxmanifest.lua using long whitespace padding so the line scrolls off-screen in editors.
Loader steals txAdmin data: txData/admins.json, txData/<profile>/config.json, server.cfg, sv_licenseKey, DB credentials, Discord tokens.
Exfiltrates via Discord webhook or HTTPS POST to a *-panel.me endpoint.
Registers a playerConnecting / deferrals handler that rejects every connecting player with an extortion message naming the panel domain.
Re-establishes access using stolen txAdmin admin credentials, stolen license key, or an admin entry it appended to admins.json - so file cleanup alone does NOT evict it.
lock_message_fragments: to nuke any other servers on fivem

families.name: Kercher Panel
behaviour: Same manifest-padding + txAdmin theft pattern as Blum; shared or forked codebase.

families.name: Generic *-panel FiveM loader
behaviour: Any resource that fetches remote code at runtime and executes it via load/loadstring/eval.

network_indicators.description: DETECTION ONLY. Do not resolve or contact. Match as substrings, case-insensitive.

manifest_indicators.why: A run of 60+ spaces/tabs before a directive hides the line beyond the editor viewport. This is the signature Blum manifest injection.
server_script(s) pointing at .js/.mjs inside a resource that is otherwise pure Lua.
Fake tooling filenames used as loader drop points inside FiveM resources.
mysql-async / lib spam blocks used to push the injected line out of view.
Large blank gap followed by content - visual hiding.
Manifest references a script that no longer exists: an incomplete cleanup, or the loader deleted itself after running.

suspicious_filenames.note: Filename alone is not proof. Correlate with code_signatures and with whether the file is referenced by a padded manifest line.

txadmin_indicators.why: An admin account you do not recognise in txData/admins.json is standing access for the attacker. Cleaning resource files does not remove it.
More than one master admin, or a master you did not create.
admins.json modified around the intrusion window.
Files inside the txAdmin bundle with modification times differing from the artifact install.
Attacker-controlled Discord bot/webhook configured in txAdmin for persistence and exfil.
txAdmin web port (default 40120) reachable from the internet without an allowlist.
A live txAdmin PIN, or Cfx.re provider auth the attacker can reuse to log straight back in.

servercfg_indicators.why: exec of a cfg file you did not author - the classic re-entry hook.
add_principal / add_ace granting group.admin or command rights to an unknown identifier.
ensure/start of a resource that is not in your inventory.
Empty, default, or reused rcon_password gives full console control.
License key, DB password, Discord and Steam API tokens sitting in a file the attacker already read.

windows.why: Attacker-added Defender exclusion paths - a near-certain compromise tell on a game server.
Scheduled task that re-downloads or re-launches the payload after cleanup.
Service binary in a user-writable directory.
WMI permanent event subscription - survives reboots and file cleanup, and is missed by most cleanups.
Attacker-created local account or an existing account added to Administrators. This alone re-opens the server after any file cleanup.
Silent remote-access tooling installed for re-entry.
Inbound allow rules the attacker added for their own access.
RDP reachable from the internet is the most common initial access route for FiveM VPS compromise.
Unexpected listeners or outbound sessions to unfamiliar infrastructure.

linux.why: Attacker SSH key = permanent access that no file cleanup removes.

database_indicators.why: Accounts granted from '%' allow remote DB login from anywhere.
Attacker granted themselves in-game admin via the framework's users/players table.
Some loaders stage Lua/JS inside a table and execute it at runtime.

reinfection_vectors.vector: txAdmin admin account left in place
reinfection_vectors.closes_with: Remove unknown admins, rotate every remaining admin password, revoke sessions, regenerate the master account.
Revoke and regenerate the key in Keymaster; the old key is attacker-usable until you do.
Rotate that password, enable 2FA, review authorised sessions and server registrations.
Rotate all host credentials, remove unknown accounts and keys, restrict management ports to an allowlist or VPN.
Rotate; never reuse; do not expose rcon to the internet.
Rotate the DB password, drop unknown accounts, remove wildcard-host grants, bind MySQL to localhost.
Regenerate the bot token, delete every webhook the attacker could have read.
The host audit in tools/ - and if any is found, treat the host as fully compromised and rebuild.

reinfection_vectors.vector: The same cracked or leaked resource re-uploaded
reinfection_vectors.closes_with: Identify patient zero, purge it, and stop deploying leaked assets - this is the single most common initial infection route.
Scan every backup before restore; date-bound your known-good backup to before first compromise.
Every person with server access rotates their own credentials and scans their machine.

reinfection_vectors.vector: Cleanup performed while the server was still running
reinfection_vectors.closes_with: Stop FXServer and txAdmin before cleaning; a live loader rewrites files behind you.

false_positive_guidance.note: These reduce noise. They NEVER clear a finding on their own - a file in an allowlisted location that also matches a critical code signature is still a finding.
known_good_js_contexts: NUI interface scripts under html/ or ui/
bundled vendor libraries (jquery, vue, react) inside html/
oxmysql, screenshot-basic and other well-known JS resources from their official repositories
false_positive_guidance.verification_rule: Before deleting any JS file, confirm it is NOT the resource's intended NUI script and IS referenced by an injected/padded manifest line or matches a critical signature.
